Ludchen v. Stelcrete Industries Ltd. 2013 ONSC 7495

HEARD at Welland, Ontario:

October 7, 8, 9, 10,
11, 18 and 21, 2013

THE HONOURABLE JUSTICE J. R. HENDERSON

rEASONS FOR JUDGMENT

Introduction

[
1
]

The plaintiff Richard
Ludchen (“Ludchen”) was a plant superintendent who worked for the defendant
Stelcrete Industries Ltd. (“Stelcrete”) at Stelcrete’s Welland plant. On
February 4, 2008, Stelcrete terminated Ludchen’s employment without notice. Ludchen
now brings this action for damages for wrongful dismissal, aggravated damages,
and punitive damages.

[
2
]

Stelcrete submits that
it had just cause for Ludchen’s termination without notice because on January
17, 2008, Ludchen made anti-Semitic remarks about the owners of Stelcrete,
Larry Cohen and Steve Cohen, in response to Stelcrete’s decision to not provide
the employees with a paid holiday on Family Day.

[
3
]

Ludchen denies that he
made any anti-Semitic remarks about the owners of Stelcrete on that day, or on
any day.  In the alternative, counsel for Ludchen submits that any such remarks
do not provide just cause for Ludchen’s termination without notice.

THE
BACKGROUND FACTS

[
4
]

Stelcrete is in the
business of making and assembling rebar for sale to the precast concrete
industry.  Stelcrete is a wholly owned subsidiary of Myer Salit Ltd., operating
under the name Salit Steel. The major shareholders of Myer Salit Ltd., and the acknowledged
“owners” of Stelcrete, are Larry Cohen and his son, Steve Cohen.

[
5
]

Ludchen started
working for Stelcrete in January 1997 as a production welder.  He was promoted
to a welding supervisor at the Niagara Falls plant in 1999.  His title changed
to plant superintendent in 2006, and he moved to the Welland plant in the same
capacity when it opened in 2007. At the time of termination Ludchen was in
charge of the rebar assembly division of the Welland plant, but not in charge of
the entire Welland operation which consisted of three separate divisions.

[
6
]

Ludchen’s duties
included supervising and directing the production welders; purchasing the steel
and consumables required for the rebar assemblies; hiring, firing, and
disciplining employees; and ensuring that production occurred in a cost
effective and safe manner.  At the time of his termination he supervised
approximately 16 or 17 fulltime employees in the assembly division.

[
7
]

Ludchen had no history
of discipline problems. By all accounts he was a respected employee, and he was
regarded as a good boss by his subordinates.

[
8
]

At the time of
termination Ludchen’s base salary was $61,000 per year. He had received a bonus
every January in the range of $2,000 to $5,000 per year from 2003 to 2008.
Ludchen had health benefit insurance coverage provided for him by Stelcrete,
and counsel agree that the cost to Stelcrete of that coverage was $542 per
month.

THE LAW

[
9
]

The onus is on the employer to prove on a balance of probabilities that
there was just cause for the employee’s termination without notice.  The task
of proving just cause is often broken down into two steps.  The employer must
prove first that there has been misconduct on the part of the employee, and
second that the misconduct justifies termination of the employment
relationship.  In that respect see the cases of
McKinley v. BC Tel,

2001 SCC 38 (CanLII)
, [2001] S.C.J. No. 40, at para.
29
, and
Geluch v. Rosedale Golf Association,
Limited,

2004 CanLII 14566
(ONSC), at para.
85
.

[
10
]

Further, whether the employee’s misconduct justifies termination of the
employment relationship requires a contextual analysis.  I accept that
insubordination by an employee, as is alleged in this case, is akin to
dishonesty, and therefore the passage set out below from para. 48 of the
McKinley

case applies:

In light of the
foregoing analysis, I am of the view that whether an employer is justified in
dismissing an employee on the grounds of dishonesty is a question that requires
an assessment of the context of the alleged misconduct.  More specifically, the
test is whether the employee’s dishonesty gave rise to a breakdown in the
employment relationship.  This test can be expressed in different ways.  One
could say, for example, that just cause for dismissal exists where the dishonesty
violates an essential condition of the employment contract, breaches the faith
inherent to the work relationship, or is fundamentally or directly inconsistent
with the employee’s obligations to his or her employer.

[
11
]

I also accept that a single incident of misconduct or insubordination
may constitute just cause for termination. See for example the case of
Wise
v. Broadway Properties Ltd.,

2005 BCCA 546
, a case in which a caretaker was
dismissed for just cause because of a letter that he wrote in which he compared
his Jewish employer to German corporations that utilized Jewish slave labour in
World War II. Also see for example the case of
Bennett v. Cunningham,

2012
ONCA 540
, a case in which a lawyer was dismissed for just cause because she
wrote a letter in which she accused her employer of being dishonest and
negligent.

THE
ALLEGED MISCONDUCT

1. OVERVIEW

[
12
]

The incident that gave rise to Ludchen’s termination revolves around the
Ontario government’s decision to create a new public holiday, Family Day, in
February of each year.  The first Family Day was scheduled to occur on February
18, 2008.  In that year Stelcrete had an option to not provide a paid holiday
on Family Day if Stelcrete provided at least the minimum number of paid
holidays required by the legislation. Stelcrete exercised that option.

[
13
]

On January 17, 2008, the Manager of Human Resources, Robin Dietsch
(“Dietsch”) sent an email to Ludchen, with an Announcement attached to the
email, and requested that Ludchen post the Announcement at the Welland Stelcrete
plant.  The Announcement informed the employees that Stelcrete would not be
recognizing Family Day on February 18, 2008, but would be providing an
additional paid holiday during the Christmas season.

[
14
]

Ludchen was in his production office at the Welland plant when he
received the Announcement from Dietsch.  Then, it is alleged by Stelcrete that
Ludchen had an angry outburst in front of his subordinates during which he
called the owners “cheap fucking Jews”, or made a similar anti-Semitic remark,
because the owners were not honouring Family Day.

[
15
]

The decision to terminate Ludchen’s employment was made by Dietsch and Robert
Nichols (“Nichols”) the General Manager of Stelcrete, but neither had any
firsthand knowledge of the alleged incident. Rather, they relied on information
that was provided to them by a private investigator, Stacey Avlonitis
(“Stacey”).

[
16
]

Stacey had been hired by Dietsch and Nichols to work undercover at the
Welland plant to investigate drug use on the job by employees, and had been introduced
to the employees as an ergonomics expert. At some point after the alleged
incident had occurred Stacey sought out Dietsch and Nichols and informed them about
Ludchen’s remarks.

[
17
]

Dietsch and Nichols did not conduct any independent investigation into
these allegations. On February 4, 2008, Dietsch and Nichols informed Ludchen
that his employment was terminated for cause without notice. At the time of
termination, Stelcrete relied solely on the January 17, 2008, incident as just
cause for Ludchen’s dismissal.

[
18
]

Stacey left her undercover job at Stelcrete in March 2008. At some point
after she left, Stacey provided Stelcrete with a written report. Later, she
sent an email dated September 2, 2008, to Dietsch in which she provided more
information about Ludchen.

[
19
]

Subsequently, in April 2013, during her examination under oath as a
witness in this action, Stacey disclosed to the lawyers for both the plaintiff
and the defendant that she had heard Ludchen make anti-Semitic remarks on
several other occasions during her undercover job at Stelcrete. As a result,
Stelcrete amended its Statement of Defence, and now relies upon this
after-acquired evidence in support of its position that there was just case for
Ludchen’s termination.

2. STELCRETE’S
CASE

[
20
]

Stacey testified that when she arrived at the Welland plant on January
17, 2008, there was a buzz in the plant among the employees. Several employees
told her that earlier in the day Ludchen had an angry outburst in response to
Stelcrete’s decision to not provide a paid holiday on Family Day. She was told that
Ludchen had slammed a door, thrown a garbage can, and called the owners “cheap
Jewish bastards”. At trial she said that everyone on Ludchen’s shift heard his
comments.

[
21
]

Stacey testified that because of this incident very little work was
being done at the plant. Accordingly, she said that later in the day on January
17, 2008, Stacey went into Nichols’ office where she told Nichols and Dietsch
what she had been told by the men in the plant.

[
22
]

Dietsch and Nichols were generally corroborative of each other, but
their version of events was slightly different than Stacey’s version. As
between Nichols and Dietsch, I find that Dietsch was able to provide more
detail. Where there is a difference between the testimony of Nichols and
Dietsch, for reasons set out herein, I prefer Dietsch’s evidence.

[
23
]

Dietsch testified that sometime in the week before February 4, 2008,
Stacey told Dietsch and Nichols that on January 17, 2008 certain employees at
the Welland plant had approached Stacey and told her that Ludchen had a “freak
out” in front of his employees and called the owners “cheap fucking Jews”
because the owners were not honouring Family Day.

[
24
]

Dietsch said that Stacey told them that she had not heard these
derogatory remarks herself, but that other employees had told her what had
happened.  Dietsch and Nichols did not arrange for a further investigation, nor
did they ask Stacey to give them the names of the employees who had given her
this information.

[
25
]

I accept that Dietsch and Nichols were astounded by such disrespectful
comments.  They believed that Ludchen was in a leadership position with the
company and a high standard was expected of him.  Therefore, after consulting
with Steve Cohen, they decided to terminate Ludchen’s employment.

[
26
]

Dietsch further testified that Dietsch and Nichols arranged for Ludchen
to meet with them on February 4, 2008 in the Niagara Falls office.  At that
meeting Dietsch informed Ludchen that his employment was being terminated.
When Ludchen asked the reason for the termination Dietsch testified that she did
not tell him the specific remarks that Ludchen was alleged to have made, but she
told him that he had made anti-Semitic remarks about the owners.  At that point
Ludchen asked if there was something that he could do to make it better, and he
was told there was not.

[
27
]

At the meeting Ludchen was given a letter that informed him of his
termination. The reason for his termination was set out in the letter as
follows, “On January 17, 2008, in front of a number of employees, you angrily
denounced a recent operational decision made by management. During this
outburst, you made anti-Semitic remarks in reference to the company’s owners”. There
were no other specific details in the letter as to the alleged remarks.

[
28
]

Dietsch testified that on the following day Ludchen telephoned her and
asked if he could speak with the Cohens. He told her that he knew what he did
was wrong and he wanted to write a letter of apology to the Cohens. Dietsch
told him that the decision had been made and that it would not do any good for
him to contact the Cohens.

[
29
]

Dietsch testified that Ludchen did not specifically admit to making any anti-Semitic
remarks at either the meeting or in the telephone call, but Dietsch said that
she believed his request to apologize was an admission.

3. LUDCHEN’S
CASE

[
30
]

Ludchen testified that he did not make any anti-Semitic remarks about
the owners on January 17, 2008, or at any time.  Ludchen testified that he
believed that he got along well with both Larry Cohen and Steve Cohen.  He felt
as if the Cohens treated him like family.  He was very excited about the new
Welland plant, and he felt as if the Cohens were putting a lot of money into
that Welland facility.

[
31
]

Prior to January 17, 2008 he knew that some of the employees had heard
that Stelcrete would not be recognizing Family Day, and that some were
concerned about that fact. On January 17, 2008, Ludchen acknowledged that he
received the Announcement in an email from Dietsch.  He was asked to post the
Announcement and he did so.

[
32
]

When Ludchen received the Announcement he testified that there were
three people in his office in the Welland plant, namely Ricky Young, Richard
James, and Wayne Juritsma.  Ludchen knew the employees would be upset about
this Announcement, but Ludchen had taken a Dale Carnegie course at the request
of Stelcrete and had learned that it was important to deal with something
negative by referring to it and then saying something positive.

[
33
]

Therefore, Ludchen testified that he told the three people in his office
that he was not happy with this Announcement.  He said that just because upper
management did not want to be with their families that did not mean that the
employees did not want to be with their families.  He then reminded the
employees that Stelcrete pays their mortgage, and that it was a great company
to work for.  Ludchen testified that his strategy worked perfectly and the
employees left his office happy and went back to work.

[
34
]

Ludchen said that he did not hear any more about this matter until he
was called by Nichols to attend at the Niagara Falls office on February 4, 2008.
At the Niagara Falls office Ludchen was told that he was terminated for cause.
When he asked the reason for his termination he said that Nichols slid a letter
to him and told him to go home and read the letter.  Ludchen testified that he
was not told what he did wrong, and therefore he took the letter home and read
it.

[
35
]

When Ludchen read the letter he said that he was devastated.  Also, he
was not sure what the phrase “anti-Semitic” meant.  He therefore called
Dietsch, but Dietsch would not tell him specifically what he had said.  He then
called Nichols who told him that he could not talk about it.

[
36
]

Ludchen further testified that when he called Dietsch he asked if he
could speak to the Cohens or write a letter to them as he wanted to apologize. At
the trial he said that he wanted to say that he was sorry that it turned out
this way, and he wanted to thank the Cohens for the eleven good years he had
with Stelcrete.

4.
CREDIBILITY

[
37
]

I had no serious problem with Dietsch’s credibility. She readily
admitted that she did not have any firsthand knowledge about the January 17,
2008 incident, and that she made limited notes. She also acknowledged that at no
time did she ever specifically tell Ludchen what he was alleged to have said.

[
38
]

My greatest criticism of Dietsch was the fact that, as the Manager of Human
Resources, she had received a very serious allegation about Ludchen’s misconduct,
and she chose to not conduct any investigation into the truth of the allegation.
She did not arrange to speak with any of the men who had apparently heard the remarks;
she did not tell Ludchen what he was alleged to have said; and she did not ask
Ludchen if he had made any anti-Semitic remarks.

[
39
]

The case law as to the extent of an employer’s duty to investigate is
unclear, but from a practical perspective, the failure of an employer to
conduct an investigation into a serious allegation makes it difficult for an employer
to later prove the allegation in a courtroom, as is obvious in the present
case.

[
40
]

I had no real concern about Nichols’ credibility, except to the extent
that he tried to corroborate Dietsch’s evidence when it was clear that he had little
memory of any of the events in question. I find that his statement made on his examination
for discovery that he had almost no memory of the meeting with Ludchen is
correct. Thus, where there is a conflict between Nichols and Dietsch, I prefer
Dietsch’s evidence.

[
41
]

Ludchen’s credibility was questionable. There were certain parts of his
testimony that were not believable. For example, his reference to a Dale Carnegie
course as the reason for his criticism of the employer’s decision simply did
not ring true. Further, his testimony that, immediately upon his termination,
he wanted to write a letter to his employers to thank them also did not ring
true.

[
42
]

If Ludchen’s credibility was questionable, Stacey’s credibility was
non-existent. I found that Stacey was argumentative and aggressive on the
witness stand. In both direct and cross- examination counsel had a difficult
time obtaining a direct answer from her. Her initial answers were often very
general, as if she were trying to avoid giving a specific answer.

[
43
]

For example, when she was asked in direct examination why she had said
that the men were afraid of Ludchen she initially replied “they told me”.  She
was then asked who told her and she said “most of the employees”.  She was
asked again who told her and she said “100 percent of the employees who worked
for him”.

[
44
]

More concerning was the fact that when she was pressed for more detail,
she provided extremely precise information about certain incidents. In fact,
she often purported to provide, without referring to any notes, exact quotations
as to what was said by the men in the plant five years ago.

[
45
]

This tendency continued throughout most of her direct and
cross-examination.  The fact that precise information was not offered by Stacey
in response to questions initially, but was offered only after she was pressed
for answers causes me to be concerned as to the reliability of the precise
information.

[
46
]

Compounding the problem, I found that Stacey’s presentation in court was
quite unusual.  She was very animated and somewhat agitated.  Often when she
provided an exact quotation from an employee she would change her voice so as
to mimic the voice of the person she was quoting.  I found this presentation to
be unprofessional, distracting, and worrisome.

[
47
]

Stacey’s lack of notes or documentation with respect to her investigation
was another troubling aspect of Stacey’s evidence.  Stacey testified that she
was a licensed private investigator who was working undercover at Stelcrete.
In that capacity one would expect her to take notes, or make notes after her
shift had concluded, so that she could provide her employer with accurate
information.  When she was asked on cross-examination if she had any notes of
her investigation she said, “I wrote a report, you should have it”.  In my view
this was an aggressive and evasive answer.

[
48
]

By way of an interlocutory motion Stacey was ordered to re-attend at an
examination under oath and bring with her all documentation with respect to her
investigation of Ludchen.  In fact, Stacey did re-attend for an examination
under oath on September 3, 2013, but chose not to bring any documentation with
her.  In cross-examination at trial she was asked whether she had brought her
documentation to trial and she said “I don’t have any documentation”.

[
49
]

On another occasion during cross-examination she said that the
documentation did not belong to her.  On another occasion during
cross-examination she said that she had made some notes, but she did not know
where they were.  On yet another occasion during cross-examination when asked
about her lack of notes she said “I was never asked to bring my notes to
court”.

[
50
]

All of this evidence causes me to be concerned about whether Stacey in
fact made any notes of her investigation, and whether she has any documentation
of the allegations that were relayed to her by the employees.  If she has
notes, why does she seem to resist producing them, and why does she not know
where they are?

[
51
]

There is also a problem with respect to what has been called Stacey’s
report.  She provided a written report to her agency, which was forwarded to
Stelcrete in 2008, sometime after March 2008.  There was resistance to the
production of this report as well.  In December 2010 the last two pages of the
eight-page report were produced.  The other six pages were produced only after
an interlocutory order was made in 2013.

[
52
]

Even with the written report there are problems.  The report is undated
and there are no dates provided for the events that are recorded in the
report.  Stacey is unable to testify now as to the date of the report or the
date of the incidents referred to in the report.  Moreover, she is unable to
provide precise evidence as to the date her investigation started or ended.

[
53
]

Still further, Stacey’s report reads as if the information contained
therein about other incidents at the plant was information that was given to
Stacey by a third party. However, on the witness stand Stacey said that for
some of those incidents described in the report, Stacey had firsthand
information.

[
54
]

When Stacey was asked in cross-examination if she understood that she
should distinguish between what Stacey directly saw or heard and what she was
told by others she replied, “No, we don’t do that.  I disagree”.  I am not sure
what to make of that answer, but it leads me to believe that Stacey quite
freely blurred the lines between direct and hearsay evidence.

[
55
]

There was another written document from Stacey that was introduced into
evidence.  This was an email dated September 2, 2008 from Stacey to Dietsch.
This email gave more details to Dietsch as to what Stacey was told by certain
employees.  This email was not disclosed until approximately 2012 and I have no
real answer as to why.  There was a long argument in cross-examination of
Stacey as to whether this email was a report or not, and that may have
something to do with the lack of disclosure.  Further, in cross-examination
Stacey said that there were other reports that she had made that have not been
disclosed, but she cannot say how many.

[
56
]

Overall, I found that Stacey was very loose with her testimony and with
her entire approach to this situation from the time she first decided to report
this incident to Dietsch and Nichols. Since that time she has contradicted
herself, and her evidence has been contradicted by others.

[
57
]

One obvious contradiction is in fact an omission. In her report Stacey
did not provide any information that she had heard Ludchen make anti-Semitic
remarks to her on other occasions. Given that the January 17, 2008 incident compelled
her to go to management with Ludchen’s remarks, Stacey must have known that similar
remarks made in other instances would be important to Stelcrete. Yet, that information
was not contained in the 2008 report, and was not revealed to anyone until
April 2013, more than five years after the fact.

[
58
]

Further, there are some distinct discrepancies between Stacey’s evidence
and that of Dietsch and Nichols. Specifically, Dietsch and Nichols both testified
that Stacey came to them about the January 17, 2008, incident approximately one
week prior to February 4, 2008, well after the incident had occurred.  However,
Stacey insisted that she went to Dietsch and Nichols about this incident on
January 17, 2008.

[
59
]

Along the same lines, Dietsch said that Stacey told her that Stacey had
been told that Ludchen had called the owners “cheap fucking Jews”, and Dietsch
recorded those words in her notes. However, on the witness stand Stacey
insisted that this was incorrect; rather she said that she told Dietsch that
Ludchen had called the owners “cheap Jewish bastards”.

[
60
]

Lastly, Stacey’s evidence as to who told her that Ludchen had made these
remarks on January 17, 2008 is so inconsistent that it is disturbing. She repeatedly
testified at the trial that “everyone on the shift” heard Ludchen make these remarks.
That statement in itself is suspect, but it becomes incredible when it is noted
that no employee who was on that assembly division shift testified in court
that he had heard Ludchen make these remarks, or that he had told Stacey that Ludchen
had made these remarks.

[
61
]

The aforementioned email from Stacey to Dietsch was intended in part to
give Dietsch the names of the persons who had heard Ludchen make anti-Semitic
remarks.  In the email Stacey gave Dietsch the names of five employees who had heard
Ludchen’s remarks.  Two of those five people, Glen Scudamore and Carmen Tice,
testified that they had never heard Ludchen make anti-Semitic remarks about the
owners on any occasion.  Further, they both testified that they did not give
any such information to Stacey.  I note that the other three persons in the list
were not called to testify at this trial.  Thus, the information in Stacey’s
email would seem to be inaccurate.

[
62
]

Even more concerning, in terms of Stacey’s credibility, was that on the
witness stand Stacey was asked to provide a list of the employees who had told
her that Ludchen had made these anti-Semitic remarks.  In direct examination
she provided a list of six names, only two of which had been included in the
list of five names that she had set out in her email.  When she was pressed in
direct examination about the names in the email she added two more names from
the list of five in the email to her list at trial.

[
63
]

Given all of these problems I find that Stacey’s credibility was very
poor.  I cannot rely on any of her testimony.

5. ANALYSIS

[
64
]

I accept that if Ludchen had an angry outburst in front of his
subordinates during which he called the owners of the company “cheap Jewish
bastards”, or made similar anti-Semitic remarks, then this misconduct may
constitute just cause for Ludchen’s termination without notice.  However, the
main hurdle for Stelcrete in this case is proving the alleged misconduct.

[
65
]

I do not accept any of Stacey’s evidence regarding the alleged
misconduct. Specifically, I do not accept her evidence as to what was said to
her by other employees, what the situation was on the plant floor that day,
what she told Dietsch and Nichols, when she told it to Dietsch and Nichols, or
what firsthand knowledge she had as to Ludchen’s conduct.

[
66
]

At trial the hearsay evidence of Stacey, Dietsch and Nichols was
admitted into evidence, not as proof of what was said by Ludchen, but only so
that the court could understand how Dietsch and Nichols made the decision to
terminate.  Thus, even if it were believable, none of the statements made by
Stacey to Dietsch and Nichols constitutes evidence as to what was said by
Ludchen.

[
67
]

Dietsch and Nichols admittedly had no direct knowledge of what occurred
on January 17, 2008 in the assembly division of Stelcrete.  The only evidence
that Dietsch and Nichols had when they made the decision to terminate was
double hearsay evidence that several employees had said something to Stacey who
repeated it to Dietsch and Nichols.

[
68
]

This brings me to the problem caused by the inadequate investigation
into this matter.  In my view, as a practical matter, it was unwise for Stelcrete
to terminate Ludchen’s employment without conducting an independent investigation
in order to assess the validity of the alleged misconduct. Further, it would have
been prudent for management to confront Ludchen with the allegations and give
him an opportunity to respond.

[
69
]

Most concerning was the fact that prior to the termination Dietsch and
Nichols never obtained the names of the employees who had direct knowledge of
what Ludchen was alleged to have said.  Again, as a practical matter, it is
important for management to know who was making allegations about the conduct
of one of their supervisors, exactly what was alleged, whether that person
worked directly under the supervisor in question, and whether that person had
any history of problems with that supervisor.

[
70
]

Having failed to thoroughly investigate this matter at the time,
Stelcrete now has great difficulty assembling the evidence to prove the alleged
misconduct on which it acted more than five years ago. Several employees from
Ludchen’s assembly division shift testified at this trial. Each of those
witnesses had some credibility issues. However, the fact remains that every
person from Ludchen’s shift who testified said that they did not hear any anti-Semitic
remarks from Ludchen and had not told Stacey that Ludchen had made any anti-Semitic
remarks.

[
71
]

Therefore, Stelcrete is left to rely upon two very small pieces of
evidence in order to prove the alleged misconduct of January 17, 2008.
Specifically, it must rely upon Dietsch’s evidence that Ludchen requested a
chance to apologize, and the evidence of Ron Burns (“Burns”). I have discounted
completely the after acquired evidence from Stacey as that evidence depends
solely on Stacey’s credibility.

[
72
]

Regarding the apology, Dietsch acknowledged that she never told Ludchen
what he was alleged to have said, and that Ludchen never admitted making anti-Semitic
remarks.  Further, Dietsch acknowledged that Ludchen was never asked if he had
made the remarks.  She took his request to apologize to the Cohens as an
admission.

[
73
]

In my view, for there to be an admission against interest in this case
Ludchen must be made aware of what he is admitting.  Given that Ludchen was
never told what he was alleged to have done, his request to apologize cannot be
taken as an admission that he made these remarks.

[
74
]

The only other evidence of the alleged misconduct came from Burns who
was a supervisor who worked at the Welland plant in the rebar division, not the
assembly division.  He said that he was in the production office in the
assembly division with approximately three to six guys when the Family Day
announcement was made.  He testified that he heard Ludchen say, “We work for
Jewish owners.  They don’t have to pay, so why would they?”

[
75
]

It should be noted that the evidence of Burns is certainly not as harsh
as the allegations made by Stacey, Dietsch, and Nichols.  Moreover, Burns
testified that Ludchen was loud, but he was not angry when he said these words.

[
76
]

More importantly, this evidence from Burns has to be scrutinized
carefully as it is evidence that came up well after Ludchen’s termination. In
fact, Burns did not come forward with this information until sometime in 2012.
He apparently did not inform anyone at Stelcrete that he had this information
until then.  I had no real explanation as to why he waited four years before
coming forward, and why he did so at that point.

[
77
]

Further, Burns is not one of the people that one would think would be
aware of this incident as he was not part of the assembly division. He worked
in the rebar division, which was in another part of the Welland plant. To
accept Burns’ evidence I would have to find that he just happened, by good
fortune, to be in the assembly division production office at the relevant time.

[
78
]

Still further, Burns’ evidence is contradicted by other pieces of
evidence. Ricky Young testified that he was present with a few other men in the
production office when Ludchen told the men about Family Day, and Young
testified that Burns was not present in the room at the time. Also, one of the
members of Ludchen’s shift, Glen Scudamore, testified that he did not even know
Burns. Lastly, in all of the lists of employees that Stacey provided, Burns was
never named by Stacey as someone who had told her about this incident. Under
these circumstances I have serious concerns about Burns’ evidence.

[
79
]

Overall, on a balance of probabilities I find that Stelcrete is unable
to prove that Ludchen had an angry outburst in front of his subordinates during
which he called the owners “cheap Jewish bastards”, or made any other anti-Semitic
remark about them.  Thus, Stelcrete is unable to prove that there was just
cause for Ludchen’s termination without notice.

DAMAGES

[
80
]

Ludchen is entitled to compensation in the form of pay in lieu of reasonable
notice of termination. The factors the court should consider in determining the
appropriate notice period where an employee is dismissed without cause were set
out by the Ontario Court of Appeal in the case of
Bardal v. Globe and Mail Ltd.

(1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24 D.L.R. (2d) 140, at page 145 as follows:

There can be no
catalogue laid down as to what is reasonable notice, in particular classes of
cases. The reasonableness of the notice must be decided with reference to each
particular case, having regard to the character of the employment, the length
of service of the servant, the age of the servant and the availability of
similar employment, having regard to the experience, training and
qualifications of the servant.

[
81
]

In the present case I have taken into consideration the fact that Ludchen
was 44 years of age at the time of the termination of employment; that Ludchen
had no discipline history; that Ludchen was in a supervisory position; that Ludchen's
basic training was as a welder; that Ludchen had been promoted twice during his
employment with Stelcrete; and that Ludchen was employed for a total of 11
years with Stelcrete. Considering all these factors I find that the reasonable
notice period for the termination of Ludchen’s employment is 12 months.

[
82
]

Ludchen requests that the notice period be extended in accordance with
the principles set out in the case of
Wallace v. United Grain Growers Ltd.
,

1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 701, because Ludchen alleges that Stelcrete acted in bad faith,
and handled his termination in an insensitive manner. The extension of the
notice period in accordance with these principles has been referred to as
"
Wallace
damages".

[
83
]

The first problem that Ludchen has with his claim for
Wallace

damages is that a request for these damages is not contained in Ludchen’s
pleadings. In my view, if a plaintiff wishes to request an extension of the
notice period for any reason, that request and the reasons for the request must
be set out clearly in the pleadings. Accordingly, I decline to extend the notice
period for
Wallace
damages for that reason alone.

[
84
]

In the alternative, Ludchen has a second problem with his claim for
Wallace

damages. In the case of
Honda v. Keays, Canada Inc.
,
2008 SCC 39 (CanLII)
, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 362,
the Supreme Court of Canada wrote at para. 59:

Moreover, in cases
where damages are awarded, no extension of the notice period is to be used to
determine the proper amount to be paid. The amount is to be fixed according to
the same principles and in the same way as in all other cases dealing with
moral damages. Thus, if the employee can prove that the manner of dismissal
caused mental distress that was in the contemplation of the parties, those
damages will be awarded not through an arbitrary extension of the notice
period, but through an award that reflects the actual damages.

[
85
]

As a result of the
Honda
decision a court is no longer able to
extend the notice period as a means of compensating an employee for bad faith
conduct by an employer. An employee may only obtain damages as a consequence of
bad faith conduct if the employee can establish that the claim satisfies the
criteria of a mental distress claim, or supports an award for aggravated
damages or punitive damages.

[
86
]

In the present case there is no evidence of any mental distress suffered
by Ludchen. Further, I heard no evidence that would support a claim for
aggravated damages, and I find that there are no grounds on which to base a
claim for punitive damages. Therefore, the claim for
Wallace
damages
cannot succeed for this alternate reason. Also, in accordance with this
analysis, Ludchen’s claims for aggravated damages and punitive damages must be
dismissed.

[
87
]

Regarding the quantum of damages, Stelcrete requests that Ludchen's compensation
be reduced because it alleges that Ludchen failed to mitigate his damages. I
disagree with Stelcrete’s submission on this point. In my view, Ludchen acted
reasonably in response to the termination of his employment as Ludchen took a
job as a production welder commencing 10 days after his employment with Stelcrete
was terminated.

[
88
]

I acknowledge that Ludchen's new job as a production welder paid less
than his job as a plant superintendent at Stelcrete, but I accept that if Ludchen
had held out for a supervisor’s job elsewhere it is very likely that Ludchen
would have been unemployed for at least several months. Further, when and if Ludchen
obtained a supervisor’s position, it is very possible that he would not have
started at the same salary as he had been earning at Stelcrete.

[
89
]

On this point Stelcrete referred to some evidence that one of Stelcrete's
customers had expressed an interest in hiring Ludchen after he had been
terminated, but that Ludchen did not pursue this possible job. I have no
criticism of Ludchen's decision. The job itself was uncertain; the duties of
the job were unclear; the salary was never discussed; and Ludchen would have
had to relocate from the Niagara Region. Under the circumstances I find that
Ludchen's decision to immediately take a job as a production welder was
reasonable.  I find that Ludchen did not fail to mitigate his damages.

[
90
]

Ludchen is entitled to the income and benefits he would have received
from Stelcrete for the 12 month period commencing February 4, 2008, less the
income and benefits he actually received from employment during those 12
months.

[
91
]

Ludchen’s base pay at Stelcrete was $61,000 per year. His average annual
bonus for the last five years of his employment was $3,400. Therefore, I find
that Ludchen's damages for the 12 month period should include his base pay of
$61,000 plus a bonus of $3,400.

[
92
]

Ludchen also claims that Stelcrete contributed an amount toward his RSP
each year, but I heard no evidence on this point. Therefore, there will be no
compensation to Ludchen for any loss of RSP contributions.

[
93
]

Ludchen also claims an amount for the loss of the health benefit
coverage provided for him by Stelcrete. It is agreed that the cost to Stelcrete
for this coverage was $542 per month. However, Stelcrete takes the position
that Ludchen is not entitled to compensation for this alleged loss as there is no
proof that Ludchen has suffered any out-of-pocket expense.

[
94
]

Stelcrete relies upon the case of
Yiu v. Canac Kitchens Ltd.
,
[2009]
O.J. No. 871, where at paras. 22 and 23
Brown J. declined to award compensation
to the plaintiff for the cost of insurance coverage where the notice period had
expired and the plaintiff had not provided evidence that he had actually incurred
any expense for the purchase of replacement insurance coverage or for matters
that would have been covered by such insurance.

[
95
]

In my view the
Yiu
decision is an anomaly that should be
restricted to its facts. The Ontario Court of Appeal has determined that an
employee’s compensation for wrongful dismissal is not restricted to salary, but
may include the pecuniary value of lost benefits. Moreover, the Court has
rejected the notion that damages should only be awarded for lost benefits if
the plaintiff provides evidence of out-of-pocket expenses. See
Davidson v.
Allelix Inc.
(1991),
1991 CanLII 7091 (ON CA)
, 86 D.L.R. (4
th
) 542 at paras.
20-21
, and
Peck
v. Levesque Plywood Ltd.
(1979),
1979 CanLII 2055 (ON CA)
, 27 O.R. (2d) 108 at paras.
14-17
.
Therefore, I find that Ludchen’s damages should include the value of 12 months
health benefit coverage at a rate of $542 per month for a total of $6,504.

[
96
]

In summary, I find that Ludchen's damages are his 12 month base pay of
$61,000, plus an annual bonus averaged at $3,400, plus $6,504 for lost health
benefit coverage, less Ludchen's income and benefits from employment during the
notice period in the amount of $35,620, for a total of $35,284.

CONCLUSION

[
97
]

For these reasons, it is hereby adjudged that Stelcrete pay to Ludchen
as damages for wrongful dismissal the sum of $35,284. The claims for
Wallace

damages, aggravated damages, and punitive damages are dismissed.

[
98
]

If either party wishes to make submissions regarding costs they may do
so in writing within 20 days of the date of this decision.
